component_findings.dependency_declaration: Recertified level 2 under the current criterion: Direct dependencies can be declared explicitly at an appropriate project/module boundary rather than inferred from ambient state. Evidence basis: Static language-level analysis of Python's dependency and import semantics, informed by inspection of sample programs in template/programs/python/micro (mb00.py-mb11.py). | Micro benchmark programs (mb00-mb11) use only the Python standard library, with no third-party package requirements observed in the readable sample set. | Python's import system is simple and uniform: import statements resolve via sys.path with no build step, no header/library linking, and no compile-time dependency graph. | CPython ships a large, batteries-included standard library, reducing the need for external dependencies for common tasks (math, collections, itertools, json, threading, etc.). | Python's ecosystem commonly relies on native-extension packages (e.g. numpy) which introduce ABI/version-compatibility complexity, and virtual-environment management (venv, pip, poetry, conda) is required to avoid global environment pollution and version conflicts. | No native language-level module/package manifest exists (no built-in equivalent of Cargo.toml/go.mod); dependency declaration is left to third-party conventions (requirements.txt, pyproject.toml), a language-design gap distinct from ecosystem-level packaging maturity. | Dynamic, duck-typed imports and monkeypatching allow dependencies to alter behavior of unrelated modules at runtime, increasing latent complexity versus statically resolved module sys…

component_findings.artifact_source_separation: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Source-level program meaning is not unnecessarily tied to a single compiler ABI, filesystem convention or host-specific build assumption. Evidence basis: Static language-level analysis of Python language/runtime design for platform neutrality, informed by inspection of sample programs in template/programs/python/micro. | CPython source code is designed to be platform-neutral: the same .py source runs unmodified on Linux, macOS, Windows and other POSIX/embedded targets given a matching interpreter, with no language-level requirement for platform-specific code. | The reference implementation (CPython) is itself a portable C program compiled per-platform; the language specification does not require any platform-specific ABI or ISA-dependent constructs in ordinary user code. | Standard library provides mostly cross-platform abstractions (os, pathlib, socket) that abstract over platform differences, with an explicit os.name / sys.platform escape hatch only needed for edge cases. | The observed micro benchmark programs (mb00.py-mb11.py) contain no platform-specific syscalls, file-path separators, or OS-conditional imports, consistent with idiomatic portable Python. | Python bytecode (.pyc) is not guaranteed stable/portable across CPython minor versions (unlike a defined bytecode ISA such as JVM class files), meaning binary artifact portability is weaker than source-level portability; this is a language/runtime design property, distinct from Ecosystem's realized supported-platform breadth. | No mandatory FFI/ABI dependency for ordinary…
